National Register of Historic Places listings in Dallas County, Texas

stops.name: Dealey Plaza
stops.description: Elm, Main and Commerce funnel together through this 1930s plaza toward the triple underpass, and the grassy knoll on its north side is exactly where it was on November 22, 1963.

stops.name: Texas School Book Depository
stops.description: The corner window on the sixth floor of this 1901 brick warehouse is the most examined vantage point in American history; the building now holds county offices and the Sixth Floor Museum.

stops.name: John Fitzgerald Kennedy Memorial
stops.description: Philip Johnson built this roofless room of seemingly floating white concrete walls a block east of the shooting, designing a quiet place to stand rather than a statue to look at.

stops.name: Dallas County Courthouse
stops.description: Everyone calls this 1892 red sandstone Romanesque courthouse Old Red, and after years as a county history museum it went back to hearing cases when a state appeals court moved in during 2024.

stops.name: Dallas Union Station
stops.description: Five railroads once fed this 1916 Beaux-Arts terminal, and it still boards Amtrak, commuter rail and DART trains beneath a recreated set of 1930s murals.

stops.name: Reunion Tower
stops.description: The lit geodesic ball that finishes every photograph of the Dallas skyline opened in 1978 and still runs an observation deck at the top.

stops.name: Dallas Holocaust and Human Rights Museum
stops.description: Opened in 2019 two blocks north of Dealey Plaza, this museum sets Holocaust history beside the American civil rights struggle behind a facade of angled concrete slabs.

stops.name: Pioneer Plaza
stops.description: A bronze herd of longhorn steers and their trail riders runs downhill across this lawn and through an artificial creek, marking the cattle trail that once crossed Dallas.

stops.name: Pioneer Park Cemetery
stops.description: Four separate 1800s graveyards merged into this rise beside the convention center, where Dallas mayors and early settlers have lain since 1849 and the last burial happened in 1921.

stops.name: Dallas City Hall
stops.description: I. M. Pei tipped this 1978 concrete wedge out over its plaza so each floor overhangs the one below, which is why the building looks like it is leaning at you.

stops.name: Dallas Municipal Building
stops.description: Lee Harvey Oswald was jailed in this 1914 Beaux-Arts city hall and shot by Jack Ruby in its basement garage; a public law school moved into the renovated building in 2020.

stops.name: Adolphus Hotel
stops.description: Beer money built this 1912 Beaux-Arts hotel: Adolphus Busch bought the old city hall, tore it down, and put up what was the tallest building in Texas for a decade.

stops.name: Magnolia Hotel
stops.description: The rotating red neon Pegasus went up on this oil company headquarters in 1934 and became the emblem of the city; the tower is a hotel now and the horse was rebuilt for the year 2000.

stops.name: Thanks-Giving Square
stops.description: Philip Johnson dropped a walled garden into this wedge of downtown and crowned it with a spiral chapel whose stained glass winds up the inside of the cone.

stops.name: Majestic Theatre
stops.description: The last survivor of Elm Street's Theatre Row, this 1921 playhouse outlived the Palace, the Tower and the Rialto and still books touring shows.

note: Dallas has never had a run, so it wins outright over every city with a turn already (Atlanta through Denver, alphabetically). The 15 stops form roughly a 1.2-mile downtown loop: the West End and Dealey Plaza cluster, south past Pioneer Plaza and City Hall, then back east along Commerce, Main, Pacific and Elm. Every address came from a Wikipedia infobox or the NRHP Dallas County table; every ZIP was looked up against the street address (Nominatim, plus the city parks page or the venue for the plazas), and none is left null. Dropped: the Neiman Marcus Building at 1618 Main St, which is a real landmark but whose flagship store closed for good in June 2026 after the Saks Global bankruptcy, so it now fails the still-in-use test. Also dropped as outside the walkable core, all verifiable if a wider Dallas batch is ever wanted: the Arts District group (Dallas Museum of Art, Nasher Sculpture Center, Meyerson Symphony Center, Perot Museum, Klyde Warren Park), Dallas Scottish Rite Temple at 500 S Harwood St, and the Deep Ellum listings. Note that Old Red is no longer a museum: the county moved the exhibits out and a state appeals court took the building in 2024, so it is a look-at-the-outside stop now. Dallas City Hall is standing and in use, but the council has been publicly weighing demolition since fall 2025 - worth re-checking before it goes into a game.
